claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi', covering the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS and is AWS-only (no multi-cloud support).
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK language support is limited to TypeScript and Python.
Pulumi supports any programming language.

With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is then executed to deploy resources, so the code you write is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas debugging AWS CDK is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because of direct execution versus CloudFormation.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
AWS CDK state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi manages state itself.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi provides built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights (product page) provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST's team often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.
Pulumi allows defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploying across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows at the linked docs page.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi has an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at /resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.

Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications; its constructs/components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier, plus potentially enterprise services and consulting.
SST's team moved from CDK to Pulumi as SST expanded beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of SST.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has repeatedly described its own architecture as built on the Pulumi engine since the rewrite shipped.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" states: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs ("What is SST") state: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis", wrote that SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed.
Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion", wrote: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside the Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`), and its platform/package.json lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.

In SST's deploy chain, SST reads `sst.config.ts` and compiles components into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs actual state, builds a dependency graph and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate resources into cloud API calls; state is written to a self-hosted S3 bucket.
Pulumi's engine owns dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs underneath SST.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem, adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, using the engine embedded the same way.
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric and Defang, like SST, expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub star count than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode, and its release cadence is unchanged.

Pulumi offers Pulumi Cloud for cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code for centrally enforced guardrails, and components for sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be used without leaving the Pulumi engine that SST already runs on.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine.

SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework, while Pulumi directly is better when needing cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across applications that SST does not expose.
The linked post "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" (/blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/) exists and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
Linked pages exist: /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/.
